fields.title: Ezra
fields.subtitle: Ezra, “Help”
fields.description: The book of the return from exile, which begins with a pagan emperor whose spirit the LORD stirred: “let them go up to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD.” Families counted home by name; an altar on its old foundations; the old men weeping and the young shouting for joy as the foundation is laid; years of opposition, two prophets, a search through the Persian archives and a temple finished at last. Then, two generations later, Ezra the scribe, who had set his heart to study the law of the LORD, to practise it and to teach it, fasting by a canal before a dangerous journey and praying a great prayer of confession for his people. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew and Aramaic given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Ezra about?
qa.answer: The return of the Jews from exile in Babylon and the rebuilding of their life in Judah. Chapters 1–6 tell how Cyrus king of Persia allowed the exiles to go home in 538 BC, how they rebuilt the altar and laid the temple’s foundation, and how, after years of opposition, they finished the temple in the sixth year of Darius, 516 or 515 BC. Chapters 7–10 jump forward some sixty years to Ezra, a priest and scribe sent by King Artaxerxes to teach God’s law in Judah, and to the crisis over marriages with the surrounding peoples that ends the book.

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Ezra, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition held that Ezra wrote it, and parts of chapters 7–9 are told in his own voice, in the first person. Many scholars think a later editor, writing perhaps around 400 BC or somewhat after, gathered Ezra’s memoir, the official Persian letters and the lists of families into the book we have, possibly the same circle that produced Chronicles, whose closing verses Ezra’s opening verses repeat. Others think Ezra himself remains the most likely author.

qa.question: Are Ezra and Nehemiah one book?
qa.answer: In the Hebrew Bible they were counted as a single book, Ezra–Nehemiah, and they tell one continuous story: the rebuilding of the temple, of the people under God’s law, and of the walls of Jerusalem. The division into two books came later, in the Christian church, and passed into printed Hebrew Bibles only in the Middle Ages. Ezra appears in both, most memorably in Nehemiah 8, reading the law aloud to the assembled people.

qa.question: Why is part of Ezra written in Aramaic?
qa.answer: Two sections, Ezra 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26, are written in Aramaic, the common language of government in the Persian empire, which the Jews of the exile also spoke. These sections are built around official letters: the complaints sent to the Persian kings, the reply of Darius, Cyrus’s memorandum found in the archive at Ecbatana, and the letter Artaxerxes gave Ezra. The rest of the book is in Hebrew.

qa.question: Why did Ezra make the people send away their foreign wives?
qa.answer: In Ezra 9–10 the leaders report that many of the people, including priests and Levites, have married women from the surrounding peoples, against the law’s warning that such marriages would turn Israel’s heart to other gods, as had happened to Solomon. For a small community just returned from an exile caused by idolatry, Ezra saw a threat to its very survival as the people of God, and the people agreed to dissolve the marriages. Christians read the episode in different ways: some as a costly act of faithfulness in an emergency, others as something the book records without holding it up as a pattern. The concern is worship rather than race, since outsiders who turned to the LORD shared the Passover (6:21), and in the New Testament Paul tells believers married to unbelievers not to seek a divorce (1 Corinthians 7:12–14).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and Aramaic and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the original beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
For Ezra had set his heart to study the law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and rulings in Israel.

— Ezra 7:10

The book of Ezra begins where the story of Israel’s kings ended: in ruins. Jerusalem had been burned by the armies of Babylon in 586 BC, the temple Solomon built pulled down, the gold and silver vessels of the LORD’s house carried off to stand in the house of a foreign god. The people of Judah had been marched east, and in Babylon they learned to sing a new kind of song: “Beside the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down; we wept as we thought of Zion.”

But the prophets had said that exile would not be the last word. Jeremiah had even named a span of time: “When Babylon’s seventy years have been completed,” the LORD would come to their aid and bring them back. The book of Ezra is the story of that coming back. It is not a story of armies or miracles, but of permits and letters, lists of families, budgets, delays, a dispute before the Persian court, and a scribe who loved the law of God. It is about how a broken people begins again.

The name Ezra means “help”, probably a short form of Azariah, “the LORD has helped”. It is a fitting name for the man and for the book. Again and again, at every turning point, the narrator steps back to say where the help came from: “the hand of the LORD his God was on him.”

One story in two books

In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah were counted as a single book, and they are best read together. The division into two came later, through the Christian church, and passed into printed Hebrew Bibles only in the Middle Ages. Read as one, the work covers roughly a century, from the decree of Cyrus in 538 BC to Nehemiah’s second term as governor of Judah, some time after 433 BC.

Its subject is the rebuilding of three things: the house of God (Ezra 1–6), the people of God under God’s law (Ezra 7–10 and Nehemiah 8–10), and the city of God with its walls (Nehemiah 1–7 and 11–13). Ezra tells the first two parts of that story; Nehemiah carries it on.

The last verses of 2 Chronicles and the first verses of Ezra are almost word for word the same. Chronicles breaks off in the middle of Cyrus’s proclamation, with the words “let them go up.” Ezra begins by telling us that they did.

Two returns, sixty years apart

The book has two halves, and it helps to know that a long gap lies between them.

  • Chapters 1–6 tell of the first return, in the reign of Cyrus, led by Sheshbazzar and then by Zerubbabel, a descendant of King David, and Jeshua the priest. They rebuild the altar and the temple, which is finished, after long opposition, in the sixth year of Darius, 516 or 515 BC.
  • Chapters 7–10 jump forward to the seventh year of King Artaxerxes and the arrival of Ezra himself, a priest and scribe sent from Babylon with the king’s authority to teach God’s law in Judah. Most date his journey to 458 BC, under Artaxerxes I; some scholars place it in 398 BC, under Artaxerxes II, and so after Nehemiah.

Ezra himself does not appear until chapter 7, and part of the second half is told in his own words, in the first person (7:27–9:15). The story of Esther falls in the gap between the two halves.

“The LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus”

The book opens with an emperor:

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, so that the word of the LORD spoken by Jeremiah would be fulfilled, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, and he sent a proclamation throughout his whole kingdom and also put it in writing: This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever among you belongs to his people, may their God be with them, and let them go up to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel; he is the God who is in Jerusalem.

— Ezra 1:1–3

Cyrus the Great had taken Babylon in 539 BC. A clay cylinder from his reign, found in Babylon in 1879, records his policy of sending conquered peoples home and restoring their sanctuaries; it does not mention the Jews, but Ezra 1 fits it well. Cyrus was not a worshipper of Israel’s God in any sense the prophets would have recognised. Yet Isaiah had called him by name, and had heard the LORD say of him, “He is my shepherd,” and speak to him as “his anointed”.

That is the first lesson of Ezra. The God of Israel is not a local god who lost his land when his people lost theirs. He moves the hearts of emperors. And he moves the hearts of ordinary people too: those who went up to Jerusalem were “everyone whose spirit God had stirred.” The same verb is used of the king and of the returning families. Behind the politics of the Persian court, the book wants us to see the hand of God.

Why the lists matter

Chapter 2 is a long list of the families who came back, town by town and clan by clan, with the totals at the end: “The whole assembly together numbered 42,360.” It is the kind of chapter readers skip. But a list like this is a kind of answer to the exile. A people that had been scattered and counted out is counted again, by name. Each family can say: we were there; we came home.

The list is honest about its edges: some families “could not show their family or their descent, whether they belonged to Israel”. That mattered, because the returning community understood itself as the continuation of Israel, the people to whom God had made his promises. The lists say that the story has not been broken off.

Weeping and shouting

The first thing the returned exiles build is not a house or a wall, but an altar. They set it on its old foundations in the seventh month and begin the morning and evening offerings again, “because they were afraid of the peoples of the lands.” Worship comes first, and it comes out of fear as much as faith.

The next spring they lay the foundation of the temple, and the priests and Levites sing in response to one another the old refrain of Solomon’s temple. Then comes one of the most moving scenes in the Old Testament:

They sang in response to one another, praising and giving thanks to the LORD: “He is good; his faithful love for Israel lasts forever.” And all the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid. But many of the priests and Levites and heads of families, the old men who had seen the first temple, wept aloud when they saw the foundation of this temple laid, while many others shouted for joy. No one could tell the sound of the shouts of joy from the sound of the people’s weeping, because the people were shouting so loudly that the sound was heard far away.

— Ezra 3:11–13

The old men remembered what had been lost. The young had never seen it and could only rejoice at what was beginning. Ezra does not say which group was right. It simply records that both sounds rose together, and that no one could tell them apart. Many readers have found in it a picture of the life of faith: gratitude for what God is doing, mingled with grief for what is not yet as it should be.

Opposition and a long silence

Chapter 4 brings trouble. The people already living in the land, settled there long before by the kings of Assyria, offer to help build: “we worship your God as you do.” The leaders refuse: “You have no part with us in building a house for our God.” The refusal can sound harsh, but the leaders feared a worship mixed with other gods, the kind that had ruined the old kingdom. The people of the land respond by frightening the builders and bribing officials against them.

Here the book confuses many readers. In 4:6–23 it leaps ahead, past the reign of Darius, to later complaints under Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes about rebuilding the city walls. This is not a mistake: the writer gathers the opposition into one place to show its pattern across the generations, and then, at 4:24, returns to where he left off:

So the work on the house of God in Jerusalem came to a stop, and it remained stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.

— Ezra 4:24

For about sixteen years the foundation lay there with nothing on it. The prophet Haggai, who preached in that second year of Darius, put a finger on what had happened in the meantime. The people had stopped building God’s house and turned to their own: “Is it a time for you yourselves to live in paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?”

Prophets, an archive, and a finished house

Chapter 5 begins again with the word of God. Haggai and Zechariah prophesy, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua set to work again. “The prophets of God were with them, helping them.” Zechariah had a word for Zerubbabel that has comforted builders ever since: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.” And another for those tempted to look down on so small a temple: “Who has despised the day of small beginnings?”

When Tattenai, the Persian governor, asks who gave them permission, the elders answer with a short sermon: “We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth.” They tell him of their sin and exile, and appeal to the decree of Cyrus. Tattenai writes to the king, and the narrator adds a quiet sentence: “But the eye of their God was watching over the elders of the Jews.”

The search through the archives turns up Cyrus’s memorandum, not in Babylon but in the fortress at Ecbatana. Darius confirms it and orders the officials who came to question the work to pay for it from the royal taxes. The temple is finished, and the people celebrate:

Then the Israelites, the priests, the Levites and the rest of the returned exiles celebrated the dedication of this house of God with joy.

— Ezra 6:16

The first half of the book ends at Passover, the festival of the first deliverance from slavery. Notice who eats it: the returned exiles, “together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the nations of the land to join them in seeking the LORD, the God of Israel.” The door is not closed to outsiders who turn to the LORD. And the half closes on joy: “the LORD had filled them with joy.”

Ezra the scribe

Ezra arrives in chapter 7 with a genealogy that runs all the way back to “Aaron the chief priest”. He is a priest by birth, but the book is more interested in what he is by calling: “a scribe well versed in the law of Moses”. The verse that opens this introduction sums him up. Ezra had set his heart first to study the law, then to practise it, and only then to teach it. The order matters. He did not teach what he had not first lived.

Artaxerxes gives him a letter of remarkable scope: silver and gold, supplies for the temple, and authority to appoint judges and teach the law of God throughout the province. Ezra’s response is not to praise the king but to bless God, “who put it into the king’s heart to bring honor to the house of the LORD in Jerusalem.” And then he speaks for the first time in his own voice: “Because the hand of the LORD my God was on me, I took courage”.

A fast by the Ahava canal

Chapter 8 lists those who went up with Ezra and tells of their preparations. When Ezra reviews the company, he finds that no Levites have volunteered, and he will not set out until some are found. Then, before a journey of some nine hundred miles with a fortune in silver and gold, he faces a problem of his own making:

I was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen to protect us from enemies on the road, since we had told the king, “The hand of our God is on all who seek him, for their good, but his power and his anger are against all who forsake him.” So we fasted and prayed to our God about this, and he listened to our prayer.

— Ezra 8:22–23

It is a very human scene. Ezra has told the king that God protects those who seek him, and is ashamed to ask for soldiers as though he did not believe it. So the whole company fasts and prays. Ezra weighs out the treasure to the priests: “You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy.” Nearly four months later they arrive, and everything is weighed again, “everything by number and by weight”. Faith in Ezra is not careless. It prays, and it also counts.

The crisis of the marriages

The last two chapters are the hardest in the book. The leaders come to Ezra to report that many of the people, priests and Levites among them, and the leaders first of all, have married women from the surrounding peoples. Why does this land on Ezra like a blow? The law had warned that such marriages would turn Israel’s heart to other gods, and that is what happened to Solomon: “his wives turned his heart to follow other gods.” The exile was the end of that road. A small community, barely re-established, could within a generation dissolve into the nations around it, and its faith with it.

Ezra tears his clothes, pulls hair from his head and beard, and sits down, stunned, until the evening offering. Then he prays one of the great prayers of confession in the Bible:

I said, “My God, I am too ashamed and humiliated to lift my face to you, my God, because our sins are piled higher than our heads, and our guilt reaches up to the heavens.

— Ezra 9:6

Ezra has not done this himself, yet he says “our sins” and “our guilt”. He stands with his people, not above them. And in the middle of the confession he thanks God for grace already given:

We are slaves, but our God has not abandoned us in our slavery. He has shown us faithful love in the sight of the kings of Persia, giving us new life to rebuild the house of our God and restore its ruins, and giving us a wall of protection in Judah and Jerusalem.

— Ezra 9:9

A crowd gathers and weeps with him, and a man named Shecaniah speaks up: “We have been unfaithful to our God by marrying foreign wives from the peoples of the land. But even so, there is still hope for Israel.” He proposes that the people make a covenant to send the foreign wives and their children away. The people gather in the open square in the ninth month, at the start of the winter rains, “trembling because of this matter and because of the heavy rain,” and agree. A commission works for three months, and the book ends with a list of the men involved, priests first.

Christian readers have found these chapters painful. Some read Ezra’s reform as a necessary, costly act of faithfulness in an emergency, when the very survival of the people of God was at stake; others think the book records it without holding it up as a pattern, noting that it reports dissent (10:15) and that its last verse dwells on the children. What the book does not do is make the issue one of race. The concern is worship: outsiders who turned to seek the LORD shared the Passover (6:21), and long before, Ruth the Moabite had become the great-grandmother of David. In the New Testament, Paul tells a believer married to an unbeliever not to seek a divorce (1 Corinthians 7:12–14). Whatever one concludes, the chapters show how seriously the returned exiles took the danger of losing God, and how much it cost them.

How to read Ezra

Ezra is short, ten chapters, and can be read in an evening. It helps to keep a rough timeline in mind: the return under Cyrus (chapters 1–2), the altar and foundation (3), the long opposition, gathered from several reigns (4), the completion of the temple under Darius (5–6), and then, after a gap of almost sixty years, Ezra’s journey and reforms under Artaxerxes (7–10).

Read it alongside Haggai and Zechariah, who preached while the temple was being built. And read it straight on into Nehemiah, where Ezra reappears, standing on a wooden platform to read the law aloud to the people.

The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition held that Ezra wrote it, and the first-person sections may well come from his own hand. Many scholars think a later editor gathered Ezra’s memoir, the official letters and the lists into the book we have. Either way, it is a book built from documents, and it reads like one.

As you read, watch for the refrain of God’s hand: on Ezra (7:6, 9, 28), on the travellers (8:18, 22, 31). Watch for the theme of joy, which runs from the shout at the foundation to the Passover. And notice how often the book turns to prayer and to Scripture at the moments of crisis. The returned exiles had no king, no army and a poor province. What they had was the word of God, and the book shows them learning to build their life on it.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and Aramaic and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few things are worth knowing before you begin.

Two languages. Most of Ezra is written in Hebrew, but two long sections, 4:8–6:18 and 7:12–26, are in Aramaic, the common language of the Persian empire’s letters and records, which the exiles also spoke. These are the sections built around the official correspondence with the Persian kings. The translation is made from both languages as they stand.

“The LORD” and “the God of heaven.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, this translation writes “the LORD”, following long Jewish and Christian custom. The Persian kings and officials speak of “the God of heaven”, a title that recurs throughout the book, and the Jews themselves use it when speaking to outsiders.

“Faithful love.” The Hebrew word hesed, God’s love that keeps faith with his covenant, appears in the song at the foundation, “his faithful love for Israel lasts forever,” and again when Ezra speaks of the favour God has shown through the kings of Persia (7:28; 9:9).

Places and measures. The Persian province west of the Euphrates, which included Judah, is called “Beyond the River”, a translation of its official name. Weights and sizes are given in modern equivalents, so the gifts for the temple are “61,000 darics of gold, about 3 tons of silver” and the temple Cyrus authorised is “about 90 feet” high.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew and Aramaic beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Ezra 1
fields.body_html:
The LORD stirs the spirit of Cyrus

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, so that the word of the LORD spoken by Jeremiah would be fulfilled, the LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, and he sent a proclamation throughout his whole kingdom and also put it in writing: This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever among you belongs to his people, may their God be with them, and let them go up to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel; he is the God who is in Jerusalem. And wherever any who are left are living as outsiders, let the people of that place help them with silver and gold, with goods and livestock, as well as freewill offerings for the house of God in Jerusalem. Then the heads of the families of Judah and Benjamin got ready, with the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred, to go up and build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem. Everyone around them supported them, giving silver vessels and gold, goods and livestock and costly gifts, besides everything that was given as a freewill offering.

The vessels of the house counted out to Sheshbazzar

King Cyrus also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken away from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his gods. Cyrus king of Persia had them brought out by Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the leader of Judah. This was their count: thirty gold basins, 1,000 silver basins, twenty-nine knives,

thirty gold bowls, 410 silver bowls of a second kind, and 1,000 other vessels.

In all there were 5,400 vessels of gold and silver. Sheshbazzar brought all of them up when the exiles were brought up from Babylon to Jerusalem.

fields.title: Ezra 2
fields.body_html:
Those who came up from the captivity

These are the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of the exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away to Babylon. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to their own town, who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum and Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:

the descendants of Parosh, 2,172;

the descendants of Shephatiah, 372;

the descendants of Arah, 775;

the descendants of Pahath-moab, through Jeshua and Joab, 2,812;

the descendants of Elam, 1,254;

the descendants of Zattu, 945;

the descendants of Zaccai, 760;

the descendants of Bani, 642;

the descendants of Bebai, 623;

the descendants of Azgad, 1,222;

the descendants of Adonikam, 666;

the descendants of Bigvai, 2,056;

the descendants of Adin, 454;

the descendants of Ater, through Hezekiah, ninety-eight;

the descendants of Bezai, 323;

the descendants of Jorah, 112;

the descendants of Hashum, 223;

the descendants of Gibbar, ninety-five;

the people of Bethlehem, 123;

the men of Netophah, fifty-six; the men of Anathoth, 128;

the people of Azmaveth, forty-two;

the people of Kiriath-arim, Chephirah and Beeroth, 743;

the people of Ramah and Geba, 621;

the men of Michmash, 122;

the men of Bethel and Ai, 223;

the people of Nebo, fifty-two;

the people of Magbish, 156;

the descendants of the other Elam, 1,254;

the descendants of Harim, 320;

the people of Lod, Hadid and Ono, 725;

the people of Jericho, 345;

the people of Senaah, 3,630.

Priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants

The priests: the descendants of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, 973;

the descendants of Immer, 1,052;

the descendants of Pashhur, 1,247;

the descendants of Harim, 1,017.

The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the descendants of Hodaviah, seventy-four.

The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 128.

The descendants of the gatekeepers: the descendants of Shallum, the descendants of Ater, the descendants of Talmon, the descendants of Akkub, the descendants of Hatita and the descendants of Shobai, 139 in all.

The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, the descendants of Hasupha, the descendants of Tabbaoth, the descendants of Keros, the descendants of Siaha, the descendants of Padon, the descendants of Lebanah, the descendants of Hagabah, the descendants of Akkub, the descendants of Hagab, the descendants of Shalmai, the descendants of Hanan, the descendants of Giddel, the descendants of Gahar, the descendants of Reaiah, the descendants of Rezin, the descendants of Nekoda, the descendants of Gazzam, the descendants of Uzza, the descendants of Paseah, the descendants of Besai, the descendants of Asnah, the descendants of Meunim, the descendants of Nephusim, the descendants of Bakbuk, the descendants of Hakupha, the descendants of Harhur, the descendants of Bazluth, the descendants of Mehida, the descendants of Harsha, the descendants of Barkos, the descendants of Sisera, the descendants of Temah, the descendants of Neziah, the descendants of Hatipha. The descendants of Solomon’s servants: the descendants of Sotai, the descendants of Hassophereth, the descendants of Peruda, the descendants of Jaala, the descendants of Darkon, the descendants of Giddel, the descendants of Shephatiah, the descendants of Hattil, the descendants of Pochereth-hazzebaim, the descendants of Ami. All the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon’s servants numbered 392.

Those who could not show their descent

These are the ones who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan and Immer, though they could not show their family or their descent, whether they belonged to Israel: the descendants of Delaiah, the descendants of Tobiah and the descendants of Nekoda, 652.

And of the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, the descendants of Hakkoz and the descendants of Barzillai, who had married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name. These looked for their entry among those listed in the family records, but they were not found there, so they were barred from the priesthood as unclean. The governor told them not to eat any of the most holy food until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim. The whole assembly together numbered 42,360, not counting their male and female servants, who numbered 7,337; and they had 200 male and female singers. They had 736 horses, 245 mules, 435 camels and 6,720 donkeys.

Some of the heads of families, on coming to the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, made freewill offerings for the house of God, so that it could be set up again where it had stood. As they were able, they gave to the treasury for the work 61,000 darics of gold, about 3 tons of silver and 100 garments for the priests.

So the priests, the Levites, some of the people, the singers, the gatekeepers and the temple servants lived in their towns, and all Israel lived in their towns.

fields.title: Ezra 3
fields.body_html:
The altar rebuilt and the offerings restored

When the seventh month came and the Israelites were settled in their towns, the people gathered in Jerusalem as one.

Then Jeshua son of Jozadak and his fellow priests, together with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his relatives, set to work and built the altar of the God of Israel, so that they could offer burnt offerings on it as it is written in the law of Moses, the man of God. They set the altar on its old foundations, because they were afraid of the peoples of the lands, and they offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, the morning and evening burnt offerings. They kept the Festival of Booths as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings, in the number the ordinance required for each day. After that they offered the regular burnt offering, the offerings for the new moons and for all the appointed festivals of the LORD that had been made holy, and the offerings of everyone who brought a freewill offering to the LORD. From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, though the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not yet been laid. They gave money to the stonecutters and the craftsmen, and food, drink and olive oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre, so that they would bring cedar logs from Lebanon by sea to Joppa, as Cyrus king of Persia had authorized them.

The foundation of the temple is laid

In the second month of the second year after they came to the house of God in Jerusalem, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak began the work, together with the rest of their people: the priests, the Levites and all who had come back to Jerusalem from captivity. They appointed the Levites who were twenty years old or more to oversee the work on the house of the LORD.

Jeshua with his sons and his relatives, and Kadmiel and his sons, the descendants of Judah, took their places together to oversee the workers on the house of God, with the descendants of Henadad and their sons and relatives, the Levites. When the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their vestments were stationed with trumpets, and the Levites, the descendants of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the LORD as David king of Israel had directed. They sang in response to one another, praising and giving thanks to the LORD: “He is good; his faithful love for Israel lasts forever.” And all the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid.

But many of the priests and Levites and heads of families, the old men who had seen the first temple, wept aloud when they saw the foundation of this temple laid, while many others shouted for joy. No one could tell the sound of the shouts of joy from the sound of the people’s weeping, because the people were shouting so loudly that the sound was heard far away.

fields.title: Ezra 4
fields.body_html:
The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin

The enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple for the LORD the God of Israel. So they came to Zerubbabel and the heads of families and said to them, “Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria, who brought us here.” But Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the rest of the heads of the families of Israel said to them, “You have no part with us in building a house for our God. We alone will build it for the LORD the God of Israel, as King Cyrus, the king of Persia, commanded us.” Then the people of the land set about discouraging the people of Judah and making them afraid to build, and they bribed officials against them to frustrate their plans throughout the reign of Cyrus king of Persia and until the reign of Darius king of Persia. In the reign of Ahasuerus, at the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the people living in Judah and Jerusalem.

And in the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and the rest of their associates wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic script and translated into Aramaic.

Rehum the chief officer and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes, as follows: Then Rehum the chief officer and Shimshai the scribe wrote, with the rest of their associates: the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the people of Erech, Babylon and Susa, the Dehavites, the Elamites, and the rest of the peoples whom the great and noble Osnappar deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River, and so on. This is a copy of the letter they sent to him: “To King Artaxerxes, from your servants, the men of the province Beyond the River. And now:

Let the king know that the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They have finished the walls and are repairing the foundations. Now let the king know that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, they will not pay tribute, tax or duty, and in the end the royal revenue will suffer. Now because we are bound to the palace by salt, and it is not right for us to watch the king being dishonored, we have sent to inform the king, so that a search may be made in the record books of your predecessors. You will find in the records and learn that this city is a rebellious city, harmful to kings and provinces, a place of revolt from ancient times. That is why this city was destroyed. We are informing the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, you will no longer have any possession in the province Beyond the River.”

The reply of King Artaxerxes

The king sent this reply: “To Rehum the chief officer, Shimshai the scribe and the rest of their associates who live in Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River: Greetings. And now:

The letter you sent us has been read to me in translation. I gave orders, and a search was made, and it was found that this city has risen up against kings from ancient times, and that rebellion and revolt have been carried on in it. Mighty kings have ruled over Jerusalem and governed the whole province Beyond the River, and tribute, tax and duty were paid to them. Now give orders to stop these men, so that this city is not rebuilt until I give a further decree. Be careful not to neglect this matter. Why let the harm grow and hurt the interests of the king?”

As soon as the copy of King Artaxerxes’ letter was read to Rehum, Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they hurried to Jerusalem to the Jews and made them stop by force of arms.

So the work on the house of God in Jerusalem came to a stop, and it remained stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.

fields.title: Ezra 5
fields.body_html:
Work on the house of God begins again

Now the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, who was over them.

Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak set to work and began again to build the house of God in Jerusalem. The prophets of God were with them, helping them.

At that time Tattenai, the governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai and their colleagues came to them and asked, “Who gave you an order to build this house and to finish this structure?”

We also asked them, “What are the names of the men who are putting up this building?” But the eye of their God was watching over the elders of the Jews, and the officials did not stop them until a report could reach Darius and a written answer about it could come back.

Tattenai’s letter to King Darius

This is a copy of the letter that Tattenai the governor of Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai and their colleagues, the officials in the province Beyond the River, sent to King Darius. The report they sent him read as follows: “To King Darius: All peace.

Let it be known to the king that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. It is being built with large stones, and timbers are being laid in the walls. The work is being carried out diligently and is making good progress in their hands.

We asked those elders, “Who gave you an order to build this house and to finish this structure?” We also asked them their names, so that we could inform you by writing down the names of the men who are their leaders.

This is the answer they gave us: ‘We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the house that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and completed. But because our ancestors made the God of heaven angry, he handed them over to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house and took the people into exile in Babylon.

However, in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, King Cyrus issued a decree that this house of God should be rebuilt. King Cyrus also took out of the temple in Babylon the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem and brought to the temple in Babylon. He handed them over to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he had appointed governor. Cyrus told him, “Take these vessels, go and put them in the temple in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its original site.”

So this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of the house of God in Jerusalem. From that time until now it has been under construction, and it is still not finished.’ Now, if it pleases the king, let a search be made in the royal archives in Babylon to see whether King Cyrus really issued a decree to rebuild this house of God in Jerusalem. Then let the king send us his decision on this matter.”

fields.title: Ezra 6
fields.body_html:
Darius finds the decree of Cyrus

Then King Darius issued an order, and a search was made in the archives where the treasures were stored in Babylon. A scroll was found in the fortress at Ecbatana in the province of Media, and this was written in it: “Memorandum:

In the first year of King Cyrus, the king issued a decree concerning the house of God in Jerusalem: Let the house be rebuilt as a place where sacrifices are offered, and let its foundations be laid firmly. Its height shall be about 90 feet and its width about 90 feet, with three layers of large stones and one layer of new timber. The cost is to be paid from the royal treasury. Also, the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem and brought to Babylon, are to be given back and taken to the temple in Jerusalem, each to its proper place. You shall put them in the house of God.”

Darius orders the work to go on

“Now therefore, Tattenai, governor of Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai and your colleagues, the officials of the province Beyond the River: keep away from there. Let the work on this house of God go on. Let the governor of the Jews and the elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its site. Moreover, I issue a decree about what you are to do for these elders of the Jews in rebuilding this house of God: the cost is to be paid to these men in full from the royal revenue, from the taxes of the province Beyond the River, so that the work will not stop. Whatever is needed, whether young bulls, rams or lambs for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, or wheat, salt, wine or oil, as the priests in Jerusalem request, must be given to them every day without fail, so that they may offer sacrifices pleasing to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons. I also decree that if anyone alters this order, a beam is to be pulled from his house and he is to be impaled on it, and his house is to be made a rubbish heap for this offense. May the God who has made his name dwell there overthrow any king or people who reaches out a hand to change this or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have issued this decree. Let it be carried out with all diligence.”

The house of God is finished and dedicated

Then Tattenai, governor of Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai and their colleagues carried out with diligence what King Darius had ordered. So the elders of the Jews went on building and made good progress, encouraged by the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo. They finished the building by the command of the God of Israel and by the decrees of Cyrus, Darius and Artaxerxes, kings of Persia. This house was completed on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius.

Then the Israelites, the priests, the Levites and the rest of the returned exiles celebrated the dedication of this house of God with joy. For the dedication of this house of God they offered 100 bulls, 200 rams and 400 lambs, and as a sin offering for all Israel, twelve male goats, one for each of the tribes of Israel. They appointed the priests by their divisions and the Levites by their groups for the service of God in Jerusalem, as it is written in the book of Moses.

The returned exiles keep the Passover

On the fourteenth day of the first month, the returned exiles celebrated the Passover. The priests and the Levites had purified themselves together; all of them were ceremonially clean. The Levites slaughtered the Passover lambs for all the returned exiles, for their fellow priests and for themselves. The Israelites who had returned from exile ate it, together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the nations of the land to join them in seeking the LORD, the God of Israel. For seven days they joyfully celebrated the Festival of Unleavened Bread, because the LORD had filled them with joy and had changed the attitude of the king of Assyria toward them, so that he supported them in the work on the house of God, the God of Israel.

fields.title: Ezra 7
fields.body_html:
Ezra comes up from Babylon

After these events, during the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of Ahitub, son of Amariah, son of Azariah, son of Meraioth, son of Zerahiah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki, son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the chief priest, this Ezra came up from Babylon. He was a scribe well versed in the law of Moses, which the LORD the God of Israel had given. The king granted him everything he asked, because the hand of the LORD his God was on him.

Some of the Israelites, as well as some of the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants, also went up to Jerusalem in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes. Ezra arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the king’s seventh year. He had set the first day of the first month for the departure from Babylon, and on the first day of the fifth month he arrived in Jerusalem, for the good hand of his God was on him. For Ezra had set his heart to study the law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and rulings in Israel.

The letter King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra

This is a copy of the letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest and scribe, an expert in the commandments and statutes of the LORD for Israel:

“Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven: Greetings. I hereby decree that any of the people of Israel in my kingdom, including their priests and Levites, who choose freely to go to Jerusalem may go with you. For you are sent by the king and his seven counselors to look into conditions in Judah and Jerusalem by the law of your God, which is in your hand, and to take with you the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely given to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem, along with all the silver and gold you may obtain throughout the province of Babylon, and the freewill offerings of the people and the priests, given willingly for the house of their God in Jerusalem. With this money, then, you are to buy without fail bulls, rams and lambs, with their grain offerings and drink offerings, and offer them on the altar of the house of your God in Jerusalem. You and your fellow Jews may do whatever seems best with the rest of the silver and gold, in keeping with the will of your God. The vessels given to you for the service of the house of your God you must deliver in full to the God of Jerusalem. Anything else needed for the house of your God that you are responsible for supplying, you may provide from the royal treasury. I, King Artaxerxes, issue a decree to all the treasurers in the province Beyond the River: whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven, asks of you is to be provided in full, up to about 3 3/4 tons of silver, about 600 bushels of wheat, about 600 gallons of wine, about 600 gallons of olive oil, and salt without limit. Whatever the God of heaven commands for the house of the God of heaven must be done exactly. Why should wrath come upon the realm of the king and his sons? We also inform you that you have no authority to impose tribute, tax or toll on any of the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants or other workers of this house of God. And you, Ezra, by the wisdom of your God that you possess, appoint magistrates and judges to judge all the people in the province Beyond the River who know the laws of your God. And you are to teach anyone who does not know them. Anyone who does not obey the law of your God and the law of the king must be punished without fail, whether by death, banishment, confiscation of property, or imprisonment.”

Ezra praises the God of our ancestors

Blessed be the LORD, the God of our ancestors, who put it into the king’s heart to bring honor to the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, and who has shown me faithful love before the king, his counselors and all the king’s powerful officials. Because the hand of the LORD my God was on me, I took courage and gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me.

fields.title: Ezra 8
fields.body_html:
The family heads who went up with Ezra

These are the heads of the ancestral families, with their genealogical records, who came up with me from Babylon during the reign of King Artaxerxes:

Of the descendants of Phinehas, Gershom; of the descendants of Ithamar, Daniel; of the descendants of David, Hattush,

of the descendants of Shecaniah. Of the descendants of Parosh, Zechariah, and with him 150 men were registered.

Of the descendants of Pahath-moab, Eliehoenai son of Zerahiah, and with him 200 men.

Of the descendants of Shecaniah, the son of Jahaziel, and with him 300 men.

Of the descendants of Adin, Ebed son of Jonathan, and with him fifty men.

Of the descendants of Elam, Jeshaiah son of Athaliah, and with him seventy men.

Of the descendants of Shephatiah, Zebadiah son of Michael, and with him eighty men.

Of the descendants of Joab, Obadiah son of Jehiel, and with him 218 men.

Of the descendants of Shelomith, the son of Josiphiah, and with him 160 men.

Of the descendants of Bebai, Zechariah son of Bebai, and with him twenty-eight men.

Of the descendants of Azgad, Johanan son of Hakkatan, and with him 110 men.

Of the descendants of Adonikam, the last ones, whose names were Eliphelet, Jeiel and Shemaiah, and with them sixty men.

Of the descendants of Bigvai, Uthai and Zaccur, and with them seventy men.

Levites found and a fast at the Ahava canal

I assembled them at the canal that flows toward Ahava, and we camped there for three days. When I reviewed the people and the priests, I found no Levites there. So I sent for Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah and Meshullam, who were leaders, and for Joiarib and Elnathan, who were teachers. I sent them to Iddo, the leader at the place called Casiphia, and told them what to say to Iddo and his kinsmen, the temple servants at Casiphia, so that they would bring us ministers for the house of our God. Because the good hand of our God was on us, they brought us a man of insight, Sherebiah, from the descendants of Mahli son of Levi, son of Israel, together with his sons and his kinsmen, eighteen men, and Hashabiah, together with Jeshaiah of the descendants of Merari, with his kinsmen and their sons, twenty men,

and also 220 of the temple servants whom David and the officials had given to assist the Levites. All of them were listed by name. Then I proclaimed a fast there by the Ahava canal, so that we might humble ourselves before our God and ask him for a safe journey for us, our children and all our possessions. I was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen to protect us from enemies on the road, since we had told the king, “The hand of our God is on all who seek him, for their good, but his power and his anger are against all who forsake him.” So we fasted and prayed to our God about this, and he listened to our prayer. Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests, together with Sherebiah, Hashabiah and ten of their kinsmen. I weighed out to them the silver, the gold and the vessels, the contribution for the house of our God that the king, his counselors, his officials and all the Israelites there had given. I weighed out into their hands about 24 tons of silver, silver vessels weighing about 3 3/4 tons, about 3 3/4 tons of gold, and twenty gold bowls worth 1,000 darics, and two vessels of fine polished bronze, as precious as gold. And I said to them, “You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy. The silver and the gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your ancestors. Guard them carefully until you weigh them out before the leading priests and Levites and the heads of the families of Israel in Jerusalem, in the storerooms of the house of the LORD.” So the priests and the Levites took charge of the silver, gold and vessels that had been weighed out, to bring them to Jerusalem to the house of our God.

On the twelfth day of the first month we set out from the Ahava canal to go to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was on us, and he rescued us from enemies and from ambushes along the way. We arrived in Jerusalem and stayed there three days. On the fourth day, in the house of our God, the silver, the gold and the vessels were weighed out into the hands of Meremoth son of Uriah, the priest. With him were Eleazar son of Phinehas and the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui, everything by number and by weight, and the total weight was recorded at that time.

The returned exiles who had come from captivity offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel: twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD.

They also delivered the king’s orders to the royal satraps and to the governors of the province Beyond the River, who then gave their support to the people and to the house of God.

fields.title: Ezra 9
fields.body_html:
The people have not kept themselves separate

After these things had been done, the leaders came to me and said, “The people of Israel, the priests and the Levites among them, have not kept themselves separate from the peoples of the lands and their detestable practices, the practices of the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites. They have taken some of their daughters as wives for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy race has mingled with the peoples of the lands. And the leaders and officials have led the way in this unfaithfulness.”

Ezra mourns and prays

When I heard this, I tore my tunic and my cloak, pulled out hair from my head and my beard, and sat down, stunned. Then everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around me because of the unfaithfulness of the returned exiles, while I sat there stunned until the evening offering. At the evening offering I got up from my fasting, with my tunic and cloak torn, and I fell on my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God. I said, “My God, I am too ashamed and humiliated to lift my face to you, my God, because our sins are piled higher than our heads, and our guilt reaches up to the heavens. Ever since the days of our ancestors we have been deeply guilty, down to this very day. Because of our sins, we, our kings, and our priests have been handed over to the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plunder, and to open shame, as we are today. But now, for a short time, the LORD our God has shown us favor. He has left us a remnant who escaped and has given us a secure hold in his holy place. So our God has brightened our eyes and given us a little new life in our slavery. We are slaves, but our God has not abandoned us in our slavery. He has shown us faithful love in the sight of the kings of Persia, giving us new life to rebuild the house of our God and restore its ruins, and giving us a wall of protection in Judah and Jerusalem.

And now, our God, what can we say after this? For we have abandoned your commandments, which you gave through your servants the prophets when you said, ‘The land you are entering to take possession of is a land made impure by the impurity of the peoples of the lands, by their detestable practices. They have filled it from one end to the other with their uncleanness. So do not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters for your sons, and never seek their peace or their prosperity, so that you may be strong, eat the good things of the land, and leave it to your children as an inheritance forever.’ After all that has come on us because of our evil deeds and our great guilt, even though you, our God, have punished us less than our sins deserved and have given us a remnant like this, should we break your commandments again and intermarry with the peoples who do these detestable things? Would you not be angry enough with us to destroy us completely, until no remnant was left and no one escaped?

LORD, God of Israel, you are righteous, for we are left as a remnant that escaped, as we are today. Here we are before you in our guilt, though because of it no one can stand in your presence.”

fields.title: Ezra 10
fields.body_html:
A covenant to send away the foreign wives

While Ezra was praying and confessing, weeping and throwing himself down before the house of God, a very large assembly of men, women, and children from Israel gathered around him, and the people wept bitterly.

Then Shecaniah son of Jehiel, one of the descendants of Elam, spoke up and said to Ezra, “We have been unfaithful to our God by marrying foreign wives from the peoples of the land. But even so, there is still hope for Israel. So now let us make a covenant with our God to send away all these wives and their children, following the counsel of the Lord and of those who tremble at the commandment of our God. Let it be done according to the law. Get up, for this matter is your responsibility, and we are with you. Be strong and do it.”

So Ezra got up and made the leading priests and Levites and all Israel take an oath to do what had been proposed. And they took the oath. Then Ezra left his place before the house of God and went to the room of Jehohanan son of Eliashib. He went there, but he ate no food and drank no water, because he was mourning over the unfaithfulness of the returned exiles.

A proclamation was sent throughout Judah and Jerusalem to all the returned exiles that they were to assemble in Jerusalem. Anyone who did not come within three days, as the leaders and elders had decided, would forfeit all his property and would himself be cut off from the assembly of the returned exiles.

The assembly in the rain at Jerusalem

So within the three days all the men of Judah and Benjamin assembled in Jerusalem. It was the twentieth day of the ninth month. All the people sat in the open square in front of the house of God, trembling because of this matter and because of the heavy rain.

Then Ezra the priest stood up and said to them, “You have been unfaithful by marrying foreign wives, and so you have added to Israel’s guilt. Now make confession to the LORD, the God of your ancestors, and do his will. Separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from your foreign wives.” The whole assembly answered with a loud voice, “Yes! We must do as you have said. But there are many people here, and it is the rainy season; we cannot stand out in the open. Besides, this is not a task for one or two days, because many of us have sinned seriously in this matter. Let our leaders act for the whole assembly. Let everyone in our towns who has married a foreign wife come at a set time, together with the elders and judges of each town, until the fierce anger of our God over this matter is turned away from us.”

Only Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah opposed this, and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite supported them. So the returned exiles did as they had proposed. Ezra the priest and certain heads of families, one for each family and all of them named, were set apart for the task. On the first day of the tenth month they sat down to investigate the matter. By the first day of the first month they had finished dealing with all the men who had married foreign wives.

Those found to have married foreign wives

These were found to have married foreign wives. From the priests: of the descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak and his brothers, Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah. They pledged themselves to send away their wives, and because they were guilty they offered a ram from the flock as a guilt offering.

From the descendants of Immer: Hanani and Zebadiah.

From the descendants of Harim: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah. From the descendants of Pashhur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Eleasah.

From the Levites: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (that is, Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer.

From the singers: Eliashib. From the gatekeepers: Shallum, Telem, and Uri.

From the rest of Israel: from the descendants of Parosh, Ramiah, Izziah, Malkijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Malkijah, and Benaiah.

From the descendants of Elam: Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah.

From the descendants of Zattu: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza.

From the descendants of Bebai: Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai.

From the descendants of Bani: Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Ramoth.

From the descendants of Pahath-Moab: Adna, Kelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh.

From the descendants of Harim: Eliezer, Isshiah, Malkijah, Shemaiah, Simeon, Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah.

From the descendants of Hashum: Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.

From the descendants of Bani: Maadai, Amram, Uel,

Benaiah, Bedeiah, Keluhi, Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Mattenai, Jaasai, Bani, Binnui, Shimei, Shelemiah, Nathan, Adaiah, Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai, Azarel, Shelemiah, Shemariah, Shallum, Amariah, and Joseph.

From the descendants of Nebo: Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Jaddai, Joel, and Benaiah. All these had married foreign women, and some of them had wives by whom they had children.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
All these had married foreign women, and some of them had wives by whom they had children.

— Ezra 10:44

Ezra does not end with a celebration. It ends with a list of names and a sentence about children. The book that began with an emperor’s proclamation and a people going home closes in a cold square in the rain, with families coming apart. It is an honest ending, and it leaves the reader with a question the book does not try to answer.

The question the book leaves with you

Is this, then, the restoration the prophets promised? In one sense, yes. The people are home; the altar smokes again; the temple stands; the law is taught. God has kept his word through Jeremiah, and he has done it by moving the heart of a pagan king. Ezra wants us to see that, and to give thanks for it.

But in another sense, plainly not. The old men wept when they saw the new foundation. The province is poor, and it is still ruled from Susa. Ezra himself prays, “We are slaves.” And no sooner is the temple built and the law brought than the people slide back toward the very sin that had sent them into exile. The returned exiles have their house of God again. What they cannot do, it seems, is make themselves the holy people the house was built for.

So the question Ezra leaves is not whether God is faithful. He plainly is. The question is what it will take for his people to be faithful in return, and whether walls, laws and reforms can ever be enough.

Where the story goes next

The next part of the same story is Nehemiah, where Ezra reappears to read the law to the whole people and a governor rebuilds the walls of the city. But the prophets of these years were already looking further. Haggai, speaking to those who thought the new temple looked like nothing, promised more than its builders could see:

“The glory of this house in the future will be greater than its glory in the past, says the LORD of Armies.”

— Haggai 2:9

A generation or two later, Malachi announced: “suddenly the Lord you are seeking will come to his temple”. The New Testament says that he did. Zerubbabel, the son of David who laid the foundation, appears by name in the family line of Jesus at the start of Matthew’s Gospel. Jesus walked in the courts of this second temple, rebuilt and greatly enlarged by Herod, and spoke of a temple that would replace it: “Tear this temple down, and I will raise it up again within three days.” John explains that he meant his own body. In him, God “made his home among us”, as he had once done in the tent in the wilderness and the house in Jerusalem.

And the problem Ezra could not solve, a people who could not keep themselves faithful, is the one the prophets said God himself would solve. Ezekiel heard the promise: “I will give you a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within you.” The returned exiles had the law in their hands. The new covenant writes it on the heart.

Where to go from here

Ezra is not often preached on its own, but its scenes have fed the church’s prayer and preaching for a long time, and some of the best of that work is in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On faith for the journey (Ezra 8). Alexander Maclaren’s sermon Heroic Faith (Ezra 8:22–23), on Ezra’s refusal to ask the king for soldiers.
  • On Ezra’s prayer (Ezra 9–10). E. M. Bounds’s Prayer and Praying Men, whose chapter “Ezra, the Praying Reformer” takes Ezra 10:1, the scribe weeping and confessing before the house of God, as its text.
  • On the return as a picture of renewal. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “Ezra: Restoration from Backsliding” reads the faithful remnant’s return as a picture of every heart that seeks a closer walk with God.
  • On the whole story of the return. The Big Story, an Ochorus Original, whose chapter “Coming Home” tells the story of Ezra 1, Nehemiah 8 and Esther 4 together.
  • On Ezra’s reading of the law (Nehemiah 8). Two sermons on what happened when Ezra opened the book before the people: Alexander Maclaren’s The Joy of the Lord and A. B. Simpson’s The Joy of the Lord, both on Nehemiah 8:10.
  • On the builders who came after. Bounds’s chapter “Nehemiah, the Praying Builder”, in the same book, and the chapter “Arrow Prayers and Long Fasts” in The Prayers Jesus Learned, an Ochorus Original, on Nehemiah’s prayers before the king.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Ezra in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then go back to the morning when the foundation was laid, when the old wept and the young shouted and no one could tell the sounds apart. Whatever was missing, the song they sang that day was true, and it is still true:

They sang in response to one another, praising and giving thanks to the LORD: “He is good; his faithful love for Israel lasts forever.” And all the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid.

— Ezra 3:11
